# Interactivity {#sec-interactivity}

{{< include ./_extensions/r-wasm/live/_knitr.qmd >}}

:::: {.slide-outcomes}
::: {.callout-note title="Learning outcomes & Chapter summary"}

1. **Use** tooltips, panning, zooming, and selections to explore a chart.
2. **Link** selections across views and **distinguish** highlighting from filtering.
3. **Bind** selections and parameters to legends, dropdowns, radio buttons, and sliders.
4. **Create** live R widgets with Plotly, including linked legends, range sliders, animations, and dropdowns.
5. **Explain** which interactions run in the browser and remain available when a figure is shared.

:::
::::

## Why bother?

An interactive figure lets readers ask questions that a static view cannot answer all at once.
They might inspect a particular observation, zoom into a region, compare selected groups,
or use one view to choose what appears in another.
This can help us explore data ourselves and let others explore a figure without writing code.

Altair describes interactions as part of the Vega-Lite specification.
The examples here run **client-side**, in the reader's browser:
they continue to work after the Python session that created them has ended.
Plotly's R HTML widgets can also provide browser-side interactions.
Other applications, such as dashboards that run Python or R callbacks when a control changes,
require a running server. The distinction is where the calculation happens, not whether
the result looks like a dashboard.

See @sec-figure-composition for arranging panels and exporting interactive HTML,
including files that work offline.

## A grammar of interactivity in Altair

We start with the cars dataset, keeping the same complete observations across the
horsepower, fuel-economy, and weight views.
All datasets in this chapter are read locally so the embedded charts contain their data.

```{python}
#| label: interaction-cars-setup
import altair as alt
import pandas as pd

interaction_transformer = alt.data_transformers.enable('default')
cars = pd.read_csv('data/vega-cars.csv').dropna(
    subset=['Horsepower', 'Miles_per_Gallon', 'Weight_in_lbs', 'Origin']
)
car_scatter = alt.Chart(cars).mark_circle().encode(
    x='Horsepower:Q', y='Miles_per_Gallon:Q'
)
```

### Tooltips

Hover over a point to inspect its car name.

```{python}
#| label: interaction-tooltip-single-alt
car_scatter.encode(tooltip='Name:N')
```

Pass a list to include several fields. Tooltips provide details on demand,
but essential explanations should remain visible without hovering.

```{python}
#| label: interaction-tooltip-multiple-alt
car_scatter.encode(tooltip=['Name:N', 'Origin:N'])
```

### Panning and zooming

`.interactive()` binds an interval selection to the position scales.
Scroll over the plot to zoom and drag to pan; double-click to reset.

```{python}
#| label: interaction-pan-zoom-alt
car_scatter.encode(tooltip=['Name:N', 'Origin:N']).interactive()
```

### Interval selections

An interval selection lets us drag a rectangle around observations.
This is often called a **brush**. The rectangle defines a selection,
but we must also specify what that selection should change.

```{python}
#| label: interaction-brush-alt
brush = alt.selection_interval(name='car_brush')
car_scatter.add_params(brush)
```

### Highlighting selected observations

`alt.condition()` chooses an encoding based on a predicate:
`alt.condition(test, if_true, if_false)`.
Here selected cars retain their origin colors, while unselected cars become light gray.
An empty selection matches all observations by default. Double-click to clear a brush.

```{python}
#| label: interaction-brush-highlight-alt
brush = alt.selection_interval(name='car_highlight_brush')
car_scatter.encode(
    color=alt.condition(brush, 'Origin:N', alt.value('lightgray'))
).add_params(brush)
```

Limit the selection to x to choose a horsepower interval regardless of fuel economy.

```{python}
#| label: interaction-x-brush-alt
brush = alt.selection_interval(name='horsepower_brush', encodings=['x'])
car_scatter.encode(
    color=alt.condition(brush, 'Origin:N', alt.value('lightgray'))
).add_params(brush)
```

### Linking selections across views

Referencing the same selection parameter in several views lets us highlight the same
observations across different encodings. This is **linked brushing**.
The first plot below uses fuel economy on y; the second uses weight.
Brush either view and inspect where those cars lie in the other.

```{python}
#| label: interaction-linked-global-alt
brush = alt.selection_interval(name='linked_global_brush')
linked_points = car_scatter.encode(
    color=alt.condition(brush, 'Origin:N', alt.value('lightgray'))
).properties(width=250, height=220).add_params(brush)
linked_points | linked_points.encode(y='Weight_in_lbs:Q')
```

The default `resolve='global'` maintains one brush: drawing in the other panel replaces it.
With `resolve='union'`, each panel can retain its brush, and observations selected in
**either** view are highlighted.

```{python}
#| label: interaction-linked-union-alt
brush = alt.selection_interval(name='linked_union_brush', resolve='union')
linked_points = car_scatter.encode(
    color=alt.condition(brush, 'Origin:N', alt.value('lightgray'))
).properties(width=250, height=220).add_params(brush)
linked_points | linked_points.encode(y='Weight_in_lbs:Q')
```

With `resolve='intersect'`, observations must satisfy the brushes in all participating views.
Try selecting a fuel-economy range and a weight range that overlap for only a few cars.

```{python}
#| label: interaction-linked-intersection-alt
brush = alt.selection_interval(name='linked_intersection_brush', resolve='intersect')
linked_points = car_scatter.encode(
    color=alt.condition(brush, 'Origin:N', alt.value('lightgray'))
).properties(width=250, height=220).add_params(brush)
linked_points | linked_points.encode(y='Weight_in_lbs:Q')
```

### Click and hover selections

A point selection chooses discrete values rather than an interval.
Click a bar below to change its opacity. Hold Shift while clicking to select several origins.
For now, the bar selection and the scatterplot brush are independent.

```{python}
#| label: interaction-click-alt
brush = alt.selection_interval(name='independent_brush')
click = alt.selection_point(name='origin_click', fields=['Origin'])
selected_points = car_scatter.encode(
    color=alt.condition(brush, 'Origin:N', alt.value('lightgray'))
).add_params(brush)
bars = alt.Chart(cars).mark_bar().encode(
    x='count()', y='Origin:N', color='Origin:N',
    opacity=alt.condition(click, alt.value(0.9), alt.value(0.2))
).properties(height=80).add_params(click)
selected_points & bars
```

Change the event to `mouseover` to select a bar by hovering instead.
Here `toggle=False` keeps one hovered origin selected at a time.

```{python}
#| label: interaction-hover-alt
hover = alt.selection_point(name='origin_hover', fields=['Origin'], on='mouseover', toggle=False)
alt.Chart(cars).mark_bar().encode(
    x='count()', y='Origin:N', color='Origin:N',
    opacity=alt.condition(hover, alt.value(0.9), alt.value(0.2))
).add_params(hover)
```

### Linking views with different encodings

To make the bar selection affect the scatterplot, use the same point-selection
predicate in the scatterplot's opacity encoding.
Selecting the field `Origin` expresses which category should match across the views,
even though origin is on the bar chart's y-axis and neither scatterplot position axis.

```{python}
#| label: interaction-linked-bars-alt
brush = alt.selection_interval(name='linked_bar_brush')
click = alt.selection_point(name='linked_origin_click', fields=['Origin'])
selected_points = car_scatter.encode(
    color=alt.condition(brush, 'Origin:N', alt.value('lightgray')),
    opacity=alt.condition(click, alt.value(0.9), alt.value(0.2))
).add_params(brush)
bars = alt.Chart(cars).mark_bar().encode(
    x='count()', y='Origin:N', color='Origin:N',
    opacity=alt.condition(click, alt.value(0.9), alt.value(0.2))
).properties(height=80).add_params(click)
selected_points & bars
```

### Legend selections

We can bind the origin selection to the legend instead of the bars.
Add it to the composed chart because both panels use the shared legend.
Click a legend entry, or Shift-click several, to compare selected origins.

```{python}
#| label: interaction-legend-alt
brush = alt.selection_interval(name='legend_brush')
legend = alt.selection_point(name='origin_legend', fields=['Origin'], bind='legend')
selected_points = car_scatter.encode(
    color=alt.condition(brush, 'Origin:N', alt.value('lightgray')),
    opacity=alt.condition(legend, alt.value(0.9), alt.value(0.2))
).add_params(brush)
bars = alt.Chart(cars).mark_bar().encode(
    x='count()', y='Origin:N', color='Origin:N',
    opacity=alt.condition(legend, alt.value(0.9), alt.value(0.2))
).properties(height=80)
(selected_points & bars).add_params(legend)
```

### Filtering rather than highlighting

Opacity changes leave all observations in the chart and in any calculated summaries.
`transform_filter()` instead removes observations from the downstream calculation.
Here the bars recount only the cars inside the brush. This is a **dynamic query**.
The filtering runs in the browser; a pandas filter performed before rendering
would not respond to the reader moving the brush.

```{python}
#| label: interaction-filter-alt
brush = alt.selection_interval(name='filter_brush')
legend = alt.selection_point(name='filter_origin_legend', fields=['Origin'], bind='legend')
selected_points = car_scatter.encode(
    color=alt.condition(brush, 'Origin:N', alt.value('lightgray')),
    opacity=alt.condition(legend, alt.value(0.9), alt.value(0.2))
).add_params(brush)
bars = alt.Chart(cars).transform_filter(brush).mark_bar().encode(
    x='count()', y='Origin:N', color='Origin:N',
    opacity=alt.condition(legend, alt.value(0.9), alt.value(0.2))
).properties(height=80)
(selected_points & bars).add_params(legend)
```

The brush changes the bar counts; the legend selection only changes opacity.
These are separate decisions in the specification.

### Overview and detail through scale domains

A selection can also control a scale domain.
Drag an x-interval in the lower S&P 500 overview to choose the time range shown above.
The overview retains the full time series, providing context for the detail view.

```{python}
#| label: interaction-overview-detail-alt
sp500 = pd.read_csv('data/vega-sp500.csv', parse_dates=['date'])
base = alt.Chart(sp500, width=550).mark_area().encode(x='date:T', y='price:Q')
brush = alt.selection_interval(name='sp500_brush', encodings=['x'])
lower = base.properties(height=60).add_params(brush)
upper = base.encode(x=alt.X('date:T').scale(domain=brush)).properties(height=220)
(upper & lower).properties(usermeta={'embedOptions': {'renderer': 'canvas'}})
```

## Interactive ggplots with Plotly

Plotly is a separate visualization library that can convert many ggplots into
interactive **HTML widgets** using `ggplotly()`.
The examples below are live in this HTML textbook: hover, zoom, click legends,
and use their controls directly. A static screenshot or PDF cannot preserve those interactions.

### Tooltips, zooming, and clickable legends

We use mammal sleep data from ggplot2. Unknown diet classifications are labeled explicitly.
The `text` aesthetic supplies the animal names used in the tooltips.

```{r}
#| label: interaction-ggplotly
library(tidyverse)
library(plotly)

sleep_data <- msleep |>
    drop_na(bodywt, sleep_total) |>
    mutate(vore = replace_na(vore, 'Unknown'))
sleep_plot <- ggplot(sleep_data, aes(x = bodywt, y = sleep_total, color = vore, text = name)) +
    geom_point() +
    scale_x_log10() +
    ggthemes::scale_color_tableau()
sleep_widget <- ggplotly(sleep_plot, tooltip = 'text')
sleep_widget
```

Hover for names, click a legend entry to hide or show its group, and drag to zoom.
The toolbar provides additional modes, including rectangular and lasso selections.
Double-click the plot to reset the axes.

### Sharing legend interactions across panels

`subplot()` combines Plotly views. These two views use the same diet groups.
We suppress the duplicate legend entries from the bar chart and request group-wise
legend toggling, so clicking one legend entry affects that diet group in both panels.

```{r}
#| label: interaction-plotly-shared-legend
count_plot <- ggplot(sleep_data, aes(y = vore, fill = vore)) +
    geom_bar(width = 0.6) + ggthemes::scale_fill_tableau()
count_widget <- ggplotly(count_plot) |> style(showlegend = FALSE)
subplot(count_widget, sleep_widget, widths = c(0.3, 0.7), titleX = TRUE, titleY = TRUE) |>
    layout(dragmode = 'select', legend = list(groupclick = 'togglegroup'))
```

Shared legend groups do not automatically create linked point brushing.
Plotly also provides [client-side highlighting](https://plotly-r.com/client-side-linking.html)
for linking individual observations with shared keys.

### A range slider

Plotly's `rangeslider()` adds a small overview for navigating a larger time-series plot.
Drag its handles or the selected range to change the time interval above.
This example uses the proportions of US births named Sam or Alex, grouped by sex.

```{r}
#| label: interaction-plotly-rangeslider
nms <- babynames::babynames |> filter(name %in% c('Sam', 'Alex'))
range_plot <- ggplot(nms, aes(year, prop, color = sex, linetype = name)) +
    geom_line()
ggplotly(range_plot, dynamicTicks = TRUE) |>
    rangeslider() |>
    layout(hovermode = 'x')
```

### Animation frames

The `frame` aesthetic identifies which observations belong in each animation frame.
`ids = country` links a country's mark across frames.
Use Play or select a year on the animation slider.

```{r}
#| label: interaction-plotly-animation
gap_plot <- ggplot(gapminder::gapminder, aes(gdpPercap, lifeExp, color = continent)) +
    geom_point(aes(size = pop, frame = year, ids = country)) +
    scale_x_log10()
ggplotly(gap_plot)
```

`frame` and `ids` are interpreted by Plotly rather than ordinary static ggplot rendering.
When comparing changes, consider whether animation or a set of static panels better
supports the reader's task: animation emphasizes movement, while panels support
side-by-side comparisons without relying on memory.

### Dropdowns in Plotly

Plotly dropdowns can update trace visibility, marker properties, and layouts.
They do not use Altair's selection-and-filter grammar; a dynamic query may require
preparing traces or using other Plotly features.
Here we prepare three measurements for each cylinder group and use a dropdown
to choose which measurement appears on y.

```{r}
#| label: interaction-plotly-dropdown
dropdown_data <- mtcars |> rownames_to_column('car') |> mutate(cyl = factor(cyl))
metrics <- c('hp', 'mpg', 'qsec')
metric_plot <- plot_ly(dropdown_data, x = ~car, color = ~cyl)
for (metric in metrics) {
    metric_plot <- add_trace(
        metric_plot, y = dropdown_data[[metric]], type = 'scatter', mode = 'markers',
        meta = metric, visible = metric == 'hp'
    )
}
metric_plot <- plotly_build(metric_plot)
trace_metrics <- vapply(metric_plot$x$data, function(trace) unique(trace$meta), character(1))
buttons <- lapply(metrics, function(metric) list(
    method = 'update', label = metric,
    args = list(list(visible = trace_metrics == metric), list(yaxis = list(title = metric)))
))
layout(metric_plot,
       updatemenus = list(list(type = 'dropdown', active = 0, buttons = buttons)),
       yaxis = list(title = 'hp'), legend = list(title = list(text = 'Cylinders')))
```

Each measurement has three traces because color splits it into cylinder groups.
The visibility mask therefore covers all nine traces, not just three measurements.
The dropdown also changes the axis title so that the selected variable remains clear.
See Plotly's [dropdown](https://plotly.com/r/dropdowns/) and
[slider](https://plotly.com/r/sliders/) documentation for more control options.

## Widgets and data-driven controls in Altair

Traditional widgets and plots can both define selections.
We will explore that connection using movie ratings.
This is the full Vega movies snapshot rather than the smaller distribution-example
dataset used in earlier chapters. We remove rows missing the fields needed by these views.

```{python}
#| label: interaction-movies-setup
movies = (
    pd.read_csv('data/vega-movies-interactivity.csv', parse_dates=['Release_Date'])
    .drop(columns=['US_DVD_Sales', 'Director', 'Source', 'Creative_Type'])
    .dropna(subset=['Running_Time_min', 'Major_Genre', 'Rotten_Tomatoes_Rating',
                    'IMDB_Rating', 'MPAA_Rating', 'Release_Date'])
    .assign(Release_Year=lambda df: df['Release_Date'].dt.year,
            Title=lambda df: df['Title'].astype(str))
    .reset_index(drop=True)
)
movies.head()
```

```{python}
#| label: interaction-movies-info
movies.info()
```

```{python}
#| label: interaction-movies-base
movie_points = alt.Chart(movies).mark_circle().encode(
    x='Rotten_Tomatoes_Rating:Q', y='IMDB_Rating:Q', tooltip='Title:N'
)
```

### A legend as a selection widget

```{python}
#| label: interaction-movie-legend-alt
select_genre = alt.selection_point(name='movie_genre_legend', fields=['Major_Genre'], bind='legend')
movie_points.encode(
    color='Major_Genre:N',
    opacity=alt.condition(select_genre, alt.value(0.7), alt.value(0.1))
).add_params(select_genre)
```

With many genres, the colors and legend become busy.
A dropdown can select a genre without assigning a different color to every category.

### Dropdowns and initial values

`alt.binding_select()` supplies the available choices.
The selection matches the chosen value of `Major_Genre`.

```{python}
#| label: interaction-movie-dropdown-alt
genres = sorted(movies['Major_Genre'].unique())
dropdown = alt.binding_select(options=genres)
select_genre = alt.selection_point(name='movie_genre_dropdown', fields=['Major_Genre'], bind=dropdown)
movie_points.encode(
    opacity=alt.condition(select_genre, alt.value(0.7), alt.value(0.1))
).add_params(select_genre)
```

Give the widget a readable label and specify an initial selection.
This version starts with Comedy selected.

```{python}
#| label: interaction-movie-dropdown-default-alt
dropdown = alt.binding_select(name='Genre: ', options=genres)
select_genre = alt.selection_point(
    name='movie_genre_default', fields=['Major_Genre'], bind=dropdown,
    value=[{'Major_Genre': 'Comedy'}]
)
movie_points.encode(
    opacity=alt.condition(select_genre, alt.value(0.7), alt.value(0.1))
).add_params(select_genre)
```

### Combining a dropdown and radio buttons

Bind different fields of one point selection to different controls.
Use a meaningful order for the age ratings; alphabetical order is not their conceptual order.
Here a film must match both the selected genre and rating to be highlighted.

```{python}
#| label: interaction-movie-radio-alt
mpaa_ratings = ['G', 'PG', 'PG-13', 'R', 'Not Rated']
select_genre_and_mpaa = alt.selection_point(
    name='movie_genre_and_rating', fields=['Major_Genre', 'MPAA_Rating'],
    bind={
        'Major_Genre': alt.binding_select(name='Genre: ', options=genres),
        'MPAA_Rating': alt.binding_radio(name='MPAA rating: ', options=mpaa_ratings)
    },
    value=[{'Major_Genre': 'Comedy', 'MPAA_Rating': 'PG-13'}]
)
movie_points.encode(
    opacity=alt.condition(select_genre_and_mpaa, alt.value(0.7), alt.value(0.1))
).add_params(select_genre_and_mpaa)
```

### Sliders: equality versus a threshold

A point selection bound to a slider matches an **exact field value**.
That can be useful, but often we want observations below or above a threshold instead.

```{python}
#| label: interaction-rating-equality-alt
select_rating = alt.selection_point(
    name='movie_rating_equal', fields=['Rotten_Tomatoes_Rating'],
    bind=alt.binding_range(name='Tomatometer: ', min=0, max=100, step=1),
    value=[{'Rotten_Tomatoes_Rating': 50}]
)
movie_points.encode(
    opacity=alt.condition(select_rating, alt.value(0.7), alt.value(0.1))
).add_params(select_rating)
```

For a threshold, a scalar parameter is simpler than a point selection.
`alt.datum` refers to fields of the current observation inside an expression.
The expression below compares each film's rating to the slider value.

```{python}
#| label: interaction-rating-threshold-alt
rating_cutoff = alt.param(
    name='rating_cutoff', value=50,
    bind=alt.binding_range(name='Tomatometer below: ', min=0, max=100, step=1)
)
movie_points.encode(
    opacity=alt.condition(alt.datum.Rotten_Tomatoes_Rating < rating_cutoff,
                          alt.value(0.7), alt.value(0.1))
).add_params(rating_cutoff)
```

The control's range, step, and starting value are separate choices.
For example, this version examines cutoffs between 10 and 60 in steps of five,
starting at 15.

```{python}
#| label: interaction-rating-slider-settings-alt
rating_cutoff = alt.param(
    name='rating_cutoff_steps', value=15,
    bind=alt.binding_range(name='Tomatometer below: ', min=10, max=60, step=5)
)
movie_points.encode(
    opacity=alt.condition(alt.datum.Rotten_Tomatoes_Rating < rating_cutoff,
                          alt.value(0.7), alt.value(0.1))
).add_params(rating_cutoff)
```

### Selecting release years

We can use the same pattern to highlight movies released before a selected year.
This still highlights rather than removes the remaining movies.

```{python}
#| label: interaction-year-slider-alt
year_cutoff = alt.param(
    name='movie_year_cutoff', value=2000,
    bind=alt.binding_range(name='Released before: ', step=1,
                           min=int(movies['Release_Year'].min()), max=int(movies['Release_Year'].max()))
)
movie_points.encode(
    opacity=alt.condition(alt.datum.Release_Year < year_cutoff, alt.value(0.7), alt.value(0.1))
).add_params(year_cutoff)
```

A slider shows the range but not where most observations lie.
It also makes the snapshot's suspicious future release years visible:
for example, historical films can appear in the 2030s. Those values warrant checking
against the source data; changing an axis format alone cannot correct a date.

### Let a plot act as the widget

A bar chart can show the distribution of releases while serving as the control.
First, click a year to highlight matching movies.

```{python}
#| label: interaction-year-click-alt
select_year = alt.selection_point(
    name='movie_year_click', fields=['Release_Year'], value=[{'Release_Year': 2000}]
)
year_bars = alt.Chart(movies).mark_bar().encode(
    x=alt.X('Release_Year:Q').axis(format='d'), y='count()'
).properties(height=60).add_params(select_year)
scatter = movie_points.encode(
    opacity=alt.condition(select_year, alt.value(0.7), alt.value(0.1))
)
scatter & year_bars
```

Now replace the point selection with an x-only interval selection.
Dragging across the bars chooses a range rather than one year.
Using the `year` time unit on the date field gives a temporal year axis.

```{python}
#| label: interaction-year-interval-alt
select_year = alt.selection_interval(name='movie_year_interval', encodings=['x'])
year_bars = alt.Chart(movies).mark_bar().encode(
    x='year(Release_Date):T', y='count()'
).properties(height=60).add_params(select_year)
scatter = movie_points.encode(
    opacity=alt.condition(select_year, alt.value(0.7), alt.value(0.1))
)
scatter & year_bars
```

The basic Altair bindings include dropdowns, radio buttons, sliders, and checkboxes.
For multi-selection, use point selections on a plot or legend; for a range,
an interval brush often communicates more context than two separate scalar sliders.

### A compact plot-based control

We can make the year selector smaller and remove nonessential axis and border details.
Here we restrict the display to 1995–2029 to focus the example.
This explicit subset is not a correction of the suspicious release dates.

```{python}
#| label: interaction-compact-year-alt
movies_fewer_years = movies.query('1994 < Release_Year < 2030')
select_year = alt.selection_interval(name='compact_movie_year', encodings=['x'])
year_bars = alt.Chart(movies_fewer_years).mark_bar().encode(
    x=alt.X('year(Release_Date):T').title('').axis(grid=False),
    y=alt.Y('count()').title('').axis(None)
).properties(height=20, width=100).add_params(select_year)
scatter = alt.Chart(movies_fewer_years).mark_circle().encode(
    x='Rotten_Tomatoes_Rating:Q', y='IMDB_Rating:Q', tooltip='Title:N',
    opacity=alt.condition(select_year, alt.value(0.7), alt.value(0.1))
)
(scatter & year_bars).configure_view(stroke=None)
```

Is the lower plot still a chart, or is it now a widget?
It both displays data and defines a selection. Its role matters more than its appearance.

### A multidimensional legend

A legend need not encode just one variable.
The following control shows genre and age rating by position and combination count by size.
It works alongside year and runtime brushes.
An observation must satisfy **all three** selections to be highlighted;
`&` combines the selection predicates here, whereas `&` between charts stacks panels.

```{python}
#| label: interaction-multidimensional-alt
top_genres = movies_fewer_years['Major_Genre'].value_counts().head(5).index
movies_clean = movies_fewer_years.query(
    "Major_Genre in @top_genres and MPAA_Rating in ['G', 'PG', 'PG-13', 'R']"
)
select_categories = alt.selection_point(
    name='dashboard_categories', fields=['Major_Genre', 'MPAA_Rating'], nearest=True
)
select_year = alt.selection_interval(name='dashboard_year', encodings=['x'])
select_runtime = alt.selection_interval(name='dashboard_runtime', encodings=['x'])

category_legend = alt.Chart(movies_clean, title='Genre and rating').mark_circle().encode(
    x=alt.X('MPAA_Rating:N').sort(['G', 'PG', 'PG-13', 'R']).title(''),
    y=alt.Y('Major_Genre:N').title('').axis(orient='right'),
    size=alt.Size('count()').legend(None),
    color=alt.Color('Major_Genre:N').legend(None),
    opacity=alt.condition(select_categories, alt.value(1), alt.value(0.2))
).properties(width=130, height=140).add_params(select_categories)
year_control = alt.Chart(movies_clean, title='Production year').mark_bar().encode(
    x=alt.X('year(Release_Date):T').title('').axis(grid=False),
    y=alt.Y('count()').title('').axis(None)
).properties(width=130, height=35).add_params(select_year)
runtime_control = alt.Chart(movies_clean, title='Running time').mark_bar().encode(
    x=alt.X('Running_Time_min:Q').title('').axis(grid=False),
    y=alt.Y('count()').title('').axis(None)
).properties(width=130, height=35).add_params(select_runtime)
scatter = alt.Chart(movies_clean).mark_circle().encode(
    x='Rotten_Tomatoes_Rating:Q', y='IMDB_Rating:Q',
    color=alt.Color('Major_Genre:N').legend(None), tooltip='Title:N',
    opacity=alt.condition(select_categories & select_year & select_runtime,
                          alt.value(0.7), alt.value(0.1))
).properties(width=300, height=300)
movie_dashboard = (scatter | (year_control & runtime_control & category_legend)).configure_view(stroke=None)
movie_dashboard.properties(usermeta={'embedOptions': {'renderer': 'canvas'}})
```

Empty selections match all observations, so readers can start with any control.
Double-click a brush to clear it, or Shift-click category combinations to select more than one.
The controls themselves summarize the fixed `movies_clean` subset; this example
changes the scatterplot's highlighting rather than recomputing all the control distributions.

The result still runs entirely in the browser and can be shared as an HTML file:

```{python}
#| eval: false
movie_dashboard.save('chart-widgets.html', inline=True)
```

Complex layouts are not always necessary during quick exploration,
but can be useful when preparing a figure for someone else to explore.
See @sec-figure-composition for the distinction between default HTML export and
offline, self-contained export.
